title: Plan a production rollout: rate limits, batching, monitoring, secrets and a fallback model
scenario: A software company will launch a support assistant next week. Live chat runs on the OpenAI API, a nightly labelling job runs on the Claude Message Batches API, and a fallback model is planned. The first rollout plan and trial logs show five weak spots. You review them in the exhibit.
exhibit:
(made-up example data)

BRIEF:
  Live chat: OpenAI API. Nightly ticket labelling: Claude Message Batches API.
  A fallback model on another vendor is planned for outages.

RATE LIMITS (launch test):
  Retry wrapper: on a 429, wait 1 s, then 2 s, then 4 s, then give up. It ignores Retry-After.
  300 workers got a 429 at the same moment, each with Retry-After: 20.
  All 300 retried together after 1 s, 2 s and 4 s, and got a 429 every time.

BATCH (first trial):
  50,000 requests sent at 22:00.
  At 04:10 the batch ended. All 50,000 results are "errored".
  Each error says: params.max_tokens: field required.
  The team saw no error when it sent the batch.

MONITORING (one live call):
  Measured by our client:  9.0 s, 1 attempt
  Response header openai-processing-ms:  1200

KEYS (OpenAI project key, expires in 3 days), rotation plan:
  step 1  revoke the old key
  step 2  create a new key
  step 3  deploy the new key to the app (takes about 10 minutes)

FALLBACK (draft):
  The second model's limit: 400,000 input tokens per minute.
  Live traffic at peak: 1,000,000 input tokens per minute.
  The plan has never been run at peak load.

questions.prompt: All 300 workers kept hitting the 429. How should the retry wrapper change?

options.text: Keep doubling the wait but start at 10 s, so that the workers all retry a little later than before.
options.explanation: Retry-After: 20 is a minimum, so the first retry at 10 s is still too early. With no random delay, the workers also still retry in step.

options.text: Add 300 more workers, so that some of them get through while the others are waiting for their retries.
options.explanation: More workers add load to the same limit. The OpenAI docs also say unsuccessful requests count toward your per-minute limit.

options.text: Wait at least the Retry-After time plus a small random delay, and cap the attempts and the total retry time.
options.explanation: Right. The OpenAI docs say to treat Retry-After as a minimum, add a small random delay so clients don't retry together, and limit both attempts and total retry time.

options.text: Retry at once, up to 20 times, because a request that fails is cheap and one of them will pass.
options.explanation: Failed requests count toward the limit, so fast retries make the jam worse.

questions.prompt: All 50,000 results came back errored six hours later. What should the team do before the next run?

options.text: Test one request of the same shape on the Messages API first; batch validation errors appear only at the end.
options.explanation: Right. Claude checks each request's params asynchronously and returns validation errors when the whole batch has ended. Its advice is to verify the request shape with the Messages API first.

options.text: Treat it as an outage of the Batches API, since a bad request would have been rejected when the batch was sent.
options.explanation: Claude validates params asynchronously, so a bad request is not rejected at send time. The error says max_tokens is missing, so the request is wrong.

options.text: Set stream: true on the requests, so that the first errors show up while the batch is still running.
options.explanation: stream: true is not supported in batch requests. Results come back as a single file.

options.text: Wait for another day, because Claude retries errored batch requests by itself until they succeed.
options.explanation: The Claude docs say to build your own retry logic. An invalid request would fail again anyway.

questions.prompt: The call took 9.0 s on the client, but openai-processing-ms is 1200. What do the numbers suggest?

options.text: OpenAI spent the full 9.0 s on the call, so the best fix is to move the chat to a smaller, faster model.
options.explanation: The header shows 1.2 s of OpenAI processing. A smaller model could trim part of that, but most of the delay is elsewhere.

options.text: About 7.8 s was spent outside OpenAI's processing, so check the network, app server and queues first.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's reference describes the header only as "Time taken processing your API request". The other 7.8 s (9.0 minus 1.2) was outside that processing: on the network, in your app, or waiting before or after it.

options.text: The two numbers must match, so the header is wrong and the client's 9.0 s is the only number to trust.
options.explanation: They measure different things. The client time includes the network and your own code; the header covers OpenAI's processing only.

options.text: The delay is output length, so ask for shorter replies. That cuts the 1.2 s of processing to near zero.
options.explanation: Output length lives inside the 1.2 s. It cannot explain the other 7.8 s, which happened outside OpenAI's processing.

questions.prompt: The rotation plan revokes the old key first. What does OpenAI's guide suggest instead?

options.text: Revoke the old key first, so that nobody can use it, then create the new one and deploy it quickly.
options.explanation: That leaves about 10 minutes of failed requests. OpenAI revokes the old key only after the new one is verified.

options.text: Set a shorter expiry date on the old key, and let it end by itself after the new key is deployed.
options.explanation: The guide's step is to revoke the old key once the replacement works, not to wait for it to expire.

options.text: Create the new key and keep the old one active for another 30 days as a spare in case of trouble.
options.explanation: A spare key that stays active is an extra secret that can leak. The guide revokes the old key once the new one is verified.

options.text: Create the replacement, update the app to use it, and revoke the old key once the replacement works.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's steps keep both keys valid during the switch, so there is no gap with a dead key.

questions.prompt: If OpenAI fails at peak and all traffic moves to the second model, what happens, and what should the team do?

options.text: The fallback pool has its own limit and takes 40% of peak. Test it at peak and plan for the other 60%.
options.explanation: Right. 400,000 of 1,000,000 tokens per minute is 40%. A fallback sends load to a pool with its own limits (our rule: test it at peak), so plan a queue or a busy message for the rest.

options.text: Nothing, because a fallback has no limits of its own when it is only used as a backup for the main model.
options.explanation: Every model pool has its own limits. At peak, 600,000 tokens per minute would hit the 400,000 limit.

options.text: The fallback takes 60% of peak. The team only needs to raise the retry count on the main model.
options.explanation: 400,000 of 1,000,000 is 40%, not 60%. More retries add load and do not add capacity.

options.text: The fallback copes, because a backup model always has a higher limit than the model it backs up.
options.explanation: The exhibit shows a lower limit, 400,000 against a 1,000,000 peak. Limits vary by model and tier.
